ICMR Institutes: From research to impact- National Institute of Virology, Pune. Indian J Med Res. doi: 10.25259/ IJMR_3319_2026 Emerging and re-emerging viral infections have repeatedly tested India's capacity for rapid diagnosis, surveillance and outbreak response. Over the past decade, the COVID-19 pandemic and outbreaks of Nipah virus disease, Zika virus infection, Chandipura virus and other vector-borne and zoonotic infections have shown that preparedness depends not only on scientific discovery, but on the ability to translate laboratory evidence into deployable diagnostics, surveillance systems and timely public-health action. Established in 1952 as the Virus Research Centre and renamed the National Institute of Virology (NIV) in 1978, ICMR–NIV, Pune, has evolved into India's premier virology institute, integrating basic research with the development of medical countermeasures, outbreak investigation and pandemic preparedness. Over the past decade, its research and scientific capabilities have contributed across this continuum from diagnostic preparedness and genomic surveillance to field-based outbreak response and the detection of emerging viral threats. It serves as the national resource centre for a network of 167 Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs) and 23 biosafety level-3 laboratories, and maintains a national repository of authenticated virus strains supporting the indigenous development of diagnostics, vaccines and therapeutics (Box). This article examines key examples from the past decade illustrating how sustained virological research and institutional capacity have supported public-health action during outbreaks while strengthening national preparedness. Building pandemic preparedness: from diagnostic science to a national response: The early COVID-19 pandemic tested whether pre-existing scientific capacity could be rapidly converted into a population- level response. India required validated diagnostic protocols, quality-assured testing and mechanisms for expanding laboratory capacity across a geographically diverse country. NIV supported standardisation of molecular testing across the VRDL network; indigenous in vitro-transcribed RNA controls provided a positive-control resource when access to such material was constrained.1,2 National laboratory surveillance expanded from around 250 tests per day in early March 2020 to 50,000 per day by end-April, with 99% of districts reporting testing by then,3 a national, multi- institutional achievement to which NIV's reference- laboratory functions contributed. NIV also drove the shift from diagnosis to molecular epidemiology and countermeasure development. Sequencing and isolation of the first SARS-CoV-2 viruses from India supported further research on diagnostics, antivirals and vaccines,4,5 while genomic surveillance characterised the B.1.617 lineage and key spike mutations during Maharashtra's second wave.6 The Institute also contributed to the development of indigenous vaccines, including the inactivated vaccine Covaxin,7,8 and the world's first approved DNA vaccine against SARS-CoV-2, and has continuously tracked emerging variants and vaccine-induced immune responses to inform booster-dose policy. A complementary translational effort saw NIV develop an indigenous IgG-based antibody assay for past SARS- CoV-2 infection, transfer the technology to industry and validate it for field use — enabling the serosurveillance studies that helped inform containment and mitigation strategy across the country.9-11 Together, these contributions illustrate a continuum from standardised 2 INDIAN J MED RES, MONTH 2026 testing and diagnostic scale-up to genomic intelligence and indigenous countermeasure development and how laboratory research can become embedded in systems for epidemic response and public-health decision-making. Responding to high-consequence zoonoses: The Nipah experience: If COVID-19 demonstrated the importance of scale, Nipah virus disease has repeatedly demonstrated the importance of speed. Across outbreaks in Kerala and West Bengal since 2018, NIV teams have combined rapid laboratory confirmation with serosurveillance of contacts and surveillance of Pteropus bat populations, extending the response beyond human case confirmation to the animal–human interface.12,13 A field laboratory established during the earliest outbreaks gave way, from 2023 onward, to a rapidly deployable mobile BSL-3 laboratory that enabled onsite diagnosis within approximately four hours during the Kozhikode outbreak.14 This capability in high-containment science and field deployment also positions NIV to strengthen national multisectoral preparedness through structured One Health mock drills such as ‘Vishanu Yuddh Abhyas’- the 2024 edition of which demonstrated the value of coordinating human-health, animal-husbandry and wildlife sectors around a simulated zoonotic outbreak with regular NIV participation in such exercises identified as a priority for strengthening interagency coordination. The significance lies not simply in faster diagnosis, but in shortening the interval between suspicion and actionable evidence and how reference- laboratory expertise can evolve into a more distributed, multisectoral preparedness model. Adapting surveillance to emerging and re-emerging threats: NIV's surveillance has repeatedly adapted to shifting viral and vector ecologies. Expanded Zika screening identified infections in newer geographical settings, as well as dengue–chikungunya co- infections. The 2024 Pune outbreak reflected this, integrating molecular, epidemiological and genomic characterisation.15,16 A decade of chikungunya serosurveillance in Pune documented rising population exposure, while genomic studies tracked viral resurgence and evolution.17,18 For Kyasanur Forest disease (KFD), phylogeographic analysis traced spread beyond its historical focus into Sindhudurg district of Maharashtra, prompting state action on vaccinating high-risk forest and health workers.19,20 A multicentre field evaluation showed high performance for a portable point-of-care assay.21 An adjuvant whole-virion vaccine candidate developed with Indian Immunologicals Ltd has now completed preclinical safety and efficacy evaluation.22 Sustained VRDL-based surveillance for respiratory illness also functioned as a sentinel for zoonotic spillover. In 2024, a routine sample led to confirmation of India's second human case of avian influenza A(H9N2), with genomic characterisation and antiviral- susceptibility testing informing risk assessment.23 NIV has similarly identified and characterised outbreaks of Chandipura virus, including India's largest, in Gujarat in 2024,24 and the aetiological agents behind India's largest Guillain-Barré syndrome outbreak, contributing directly to outbreak containment.25 Diagnostic development also kept pace with newly emerging global threats: indigenous IgM/IgG ELISAs for mpox virus extended national testing capacity for this newly emerging orthopoxvirus.26 Together, these examples show how NIV's surveillance has evolved from confirming known threats to detecting the unexpected, serology tracking population exposure, genomics tracing viral spread, and routine networks doubling as sentinels for emerging pathogens. elements_zh.main_results: 应对高后果性人兽共患病:尼帕病毒的经验:如果说 COVID-19 展示了规模的重要性,那么尼帕病毒病则反复证明了速度的重要性。

elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 其重要性不仅在于更快的检测,还在于缩短从怀疑到可操作证据的时间间隔,以及参考实验室专业知识如何演变为更分散、多部门的准备模式。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 印度需要经过验证的诊断协议、质量保证的检测以及在地理上多样化的国家范围内扩展实验室能力的机制。

analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 自2018年以来,在印度喀拉拉邦和西孟加拉邦的疫情中,NIV团队结合了快速的实验室确认、接触者的血清流行病学监测以及Pteropus蝙蝠种群的监测,将响应范围扩展到人类病例确认之外的人兽共患病界面。12,13 在疫情初期建立的现场实验室,从2023年起演变为可快速部署的移动BSL-3实验室,使在Kozhikode疫情期间能够在大约四小时内进行现场检测。14 这种在高安全级别科学和现场部署方面的能力也使NIV能够通过结构化的‘One Health’模拟演练,如‘Vishanu Yuddh Abhyas’,加强国家多部门的准备。2024年的版本展示了协调人类健康、畜牧业和野生动物部门在模拟人兽共患病中的价值,而NIV在这些演练中的持续参与被确定为加强跨部门协调的关键优先事项。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 其重要性不仅在于更快的检测,还在于缩短从怀疑到可操作证据的时间间隔,以及参考实验室专业知识如何演变为更分散、多部门的准备模式。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 印度需要经过验证的诊断协议、质量保证的检测以及在地理上多样化的国家范围内扩展实验室能力的机制。

papers.title: Structural basis for substrate-assisted catalysis and small-molecule inhibition of alphavirus macrodomains
papers.abstract: Abstract Sporadic alphavirus infections are pandemic threats that evade innate immunity via macrodomains which remove host mono-ADP-ribose (ADPr). Through high-resolution crystallography of apo and ADPr-bound forms, we here define a conserved MacroD-like fold and a shared hydrogen-bonding network for macrodomains from Eastern equine encephalitis (EEEV), Venezuelan equine encephalitis (VEEV), and Chikungunya (CHIKV) alphaviruses. Our detailed active site structures support a substrate-assisted hydrolysis mechanism where the ADPr α-phosphate activates the catalytic water for nucleophilic attack. Furthermore, we identify the suramin trisulfonic moiety as a potent inhibitor. Crystal structures with solution-state SAXS show suramin occupies the ADPr-binding pocket and induces reversible, inhibitor-mediated oligomerization. Biophysical and enzymatic assays confirm low-micromolar inhibition of EEEV glycohydrolase activity, while cell-based trans -replication assays demonstrate broad-spectrum suppression of EEEV, VEEV, and CHIKV replication. Collectively, our findings define the structural basis for alphaviral macrodomain catalysis, key alphaviral macrodomain druggable features, and a promising scaffold for targeted broad-spectrum antiviral therapeutics.

papers.title_zh: α病毒宏域底物辅助催化和小分子抑制的结构基础
papers.source_body_en: Abstract Sporadic alphavirus infections are pandemic threats that evade innate immunity via macrodomains which remove host mono-ADP-ribose (ADPr). Through high-resolution crystallography of apo and ADPr-bound forms, we here define a conserved MacroD-like fold and a shared hydrogen-bonding network for macrodomains from Eastern equine encephalitis (EEEV), Venezuelan equine encephalitis (VEEV), and Chikungunya (CHIKV) alphaviruses. Our detailed active site structures support a substrate-assisted hydrolysis mechanism where the ADPr α-phosphate activates the catalytic water for nucleophilic attack. Furthermore, we identify the suramin trisulfonic moiety as a potent inhibitor. Crystal structures with solution-state SAXS show suramin occupies the ADPr-binding pocket and induces reversible, inhibitor-mediated oligomerization. Biophysical and enzymatic assays confirm low-micromolar inhibition of EEEV glycohydrolase activity, while cell-based trans -replication assays demonstrate broad-spectrum suppression of EEEV, VEEV, and CHIKV replication. Collectively, our findings define the structural basis for alphaviral macrodomain catalysis, key alphaviral macrodomain druggable features, and a promising scaffold for targeted broad-spectrum antiviral therapeutics.
papers.abstract_zh: 摘要 偶发的α病毒感染是全球性威胁,它们通过宏域去除宿主单ADP核糖(ADPr)来逃避免疫系统的先天免疫。通过高分辨率晶体学分析apo形式和ADPr结合形式,我们在此定义了来自东方马脑炎病毒(EEEV)、委内瑞拉马脑炎病毒(VEEV)和基孔肯雅病毒(CHIKV)α病毒的宏域所共有的MacroD样折叠结构和共享的氢键网络。我们的详细活性位点结构支持了一种底物辅助水解机制,其中ADPr的α-磷酸基团激活催化水以进行亲核攻击。此外,我们鉴定了suramin三磺酸基团作为强效抑制剂。结合溶液状态的SAXS晶体结构显示,suramin占据ADPr结合口袋并诱导可逆的、抑制剂介导的寡聚化。生物物理和酶活性实验确认了suramin对EEEV糖基水解酶活性的低微摩尔级抑制作用,而基于细胞的trans-复制实验则展示了其对EEEV、VEEV和CHIKV复制的广谱抑制作用。综上所述,我们的研究结果定义了α病毒宏域催化的结构基础、关键的α病毒宏域可药性特征以及一种有前景的靶向广谱抗病毒药物治疗药物的骨架。

papers.title: Aedes aegypti Abundance, Distribution, and habitat Characteristics in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania Measured Through Two-Year Longitudinal Survey of Larval and Adult Sampling Methods
papers.abstract: Aedes aegypti, the primary vector of dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever viruses, is widely distributed globally and has become a major public health concern. This study assessed the density, spatiotemporal distribution, and breeding habitat characteristics of Ae. aegypti in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. A two-year longitudinal survey was conducted in Ilala, Kinondoni, and Temeke districts. Immature and adult mosquitoes were sampled using larval dipping, Prokopack aspiration, ovitraps, and BG-Sentinel traps in four wards per district, 20 households per ward and all other potential breeding habitats in a selected ward. 220,947 mosquitoes were collected, and 8,496 (3.8%) were Ae. Temeke district had significantly higher Ae. aegypti density than the other districts (IRR=2.13, 95%CI:1.75–2.59;p<0.001), accounting for approximately 50% of all specimens collected. Mosquito density was nearly twice as high during the wet season as during the dry season (IRR=1.85, 95%CI:1.54–2.05;p<0.001). The highest Container Index (CI), House Index (HI) and Breteau Index (BI) of 14%, 3.4% and 11.9 respectively were recorded in Kinondoni district. Water storage containers exhibited the highest larval positivity rate. Aedes aegypti is widely distributed across Dar es Salaam. Water storage containers likely sustain year-round populations and represent important targets for surveillance and vector control interventions.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to assess the density, spatiotemporal distribution, and breeding habitat characteristics of Aedes aegypti, the primary vector of chikungunya virus, in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, to inform public health strategies.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A two-year longitudinal survey was conducted in Ilala, Kinondoni, and Temeke districts, focusing on four wards per district, 20 households per ward, and all potential breeding habitats in a selected ward.
analysis.methods: Immature and adult mosquitoes were sampled using larval dipping, Prokopack aspiration, ovitraps, and BG-Sentinel traps to evaluate density and habitat characteristics.
analysis.main_results: Temeke district had significantly higher Ae. aegypti density than the other districts (IRR=2.13, 95%CI:1.75–2.59;p<0.001), accounting for approximately 50% of all specimens collected. Mosquito density was nearly twice as high during the wet season as during the dry season (IRR=1.85, 95%CI:1.54–2.05;p<0.001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights the importance of water storage containers in sustaining Ae. aegypti populations and suggests they are key targets for surveillance and vector control interventions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide critical insights into the spatial and temporal dynamics of Ae. aegypti, which can inform targeted vector control strategies to mitigate the spread of chikungunya virus.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its focus on Ae. aegypti density and habitat characteristics without direct linkage to chikungunya virus transmission, and the evidence is moderate in strength due to the absence of specific viral data.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted a two-year longitudinal survey in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, to assess the density, spatiotemporal distribution, and breeding habitats of Aedes aegypti, the primary vector of chikungunya virus. The research focused on three districts, employing larval dipping, Prokopack aspiration, ovitraps, and BG-Sentinel traps to collect data. Results showed that Temeke district had significantly higher Ae. aegypti density than the other districts, accounting for about 50% of all specimens. Mosquito density was nearly twice as high during the wet season compared to the dry season. The study suggests that water storage containers are important for sustaining Ae. aegypti populations and should be targeted for surveillance and control. However, the findings are limited to Ae. aegypti density and habitat characteristics without direct evidence on chikungunya virus transmission, resulting in moderate confidence in the implications for public health.

elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果提供了关于伊蚊空间和时间动态的关键见解,可以指导针对伊蚊媒介控制策略,以减轻基孔肯雅病毒的传播。

Key points Chikungunya virus disease (chikungunya) is a nationally notifiable condition. The most recent locally acquired case was reported from a U.S. state in 2025. Chikungunya virus in the United States Before 2006, chikungunya was rarely identified in U.S. travelers. During 2006–2013, an average of 28 people per year in the United States tested positive for recent chikungunya virus infection. All were travelers visiting or returning to the United States from affected areas in Asia, Africa, or the Indian Ocean. In late 2013, the first local transmission of chikungunya virus in the Americas was identified in Caribbean countries and territories. Local transmission means that mosquitoes in the area have been infected with the virus and are spreading it to people. Beginning in 2014, chikungunya was reported among U.S. travelers returning from affected areas in the Americas, and local transmission was identified in Florida, Texas, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands. Chikungunya became a nationally notifiable condition in 2015. Cases are reported to CDC by state and local health departments using standard case definitions. The most recent locally acquired case was reported from a U.S. state in 2025. Chikungunya cases by year 2026 U.S. chikungunya cases* reported to ArboNET Data are preliminary and subject to change. news.source_body_en: The CDC report on Chikungunya virus in the United States highlights that the most recent locally acquired case was reported in 2026, with 116 travel-associated cases documented. Chikungunya became a nationally notifiable condition in 2015, and data are preliminary and subject to change. The report notes that local transmission has occurred in Florida, Texas, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. territories. The information was last reviewed by subject matter experts on September 16, 2026, ensuring its accuracy. The CDC provides updated data and resources for prevention and awareness, emphasizing the importance of monitoring and reporting for public health preparedness.
news.content_zh: 美国疾病控制与预防中心(CDC)关于美国境内基孔肯雅热的报告指出,最近的本地感染病例是在2026年报告的,共有116例旅行相关病例被记录。基孔肯雅热自2015年起成为全国法定报告疾病,数据为初步数据,可能会有所变动。报告指出,基孔肯雅热的本地传播已在美国佛罗里达州、德克萨斯州、波多黎各以及美国领土发生。该页面的信息由主题专家于2026年9月16日最后审核,确保其准确性。CDC提供更新的数据和预防与意识资源,强调监测和报告对于公共卫生准备的重要性。

news.content: 投稿 ログイン 会員登録 SYSTEM NOTICE Auto translation by AI. Be sure, accuracy, nuances and authorial intent may not be fully reflected. Show original 🇨🇳 China CDC September 2026 Risk Assessment | Focus on Dengue and Chikungunya satosilog 2026年9月19日 12:15 The Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (China CDC) has released its monthly risk assessment regarding public health emergencies and infectious diseases to be monitored in mainland China for September 2026. Since April 2011, the China CDC has been reviewing domestic and international public health emergencies, surveillance data on key infectious diseases, and information from relevant departments to assess risks for the following month, with the participation of CDC experts from each province. This time, dengue fever and chikungunya were listed as the 'key focus' for September, meaning they are the diseases requiring the most attention. In addition, Zika virus infection, mpox, human-infected novel subtype influenza, severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), cholera, malaria, and Ebola virus disease are categorized as 'general focus'. Top priority is dengue fever and chikungunya In August 2026, 267 imported cases of dengue fever were reported in China. The main sources of these imports were Cambodia, Vietnam, Laos, Thailand, and Malaysia. Furthermore, domestic infections have been reported in eight provincial-level administrative regions: Guangxi, Guangdong, Chongqing, Yunnan, Fujian, Zhejiang, Hunan, and Henan. Regarding chikungunya, three imported cases were reported in August, with Indonesia and Vietnam as the sources. Meanwhile, domestic cases have been confirmed in Guangdong, Fujian, Guangxi, and Hubei. The China CDC assesses that the risk of importation from abroad will persist in September, as the mosquito activity season continues and high temperatures and precipitation facilitate the increase of vector mosquitoes. It states that the risk of domestic infection and outbreaks remains high, especially in areas with weak mosquito control measures. Interesting here is China's 2026 'Dengue and Chikungunya Prevention and Control Plan.' This plan even sets time-based goals for 'what to do within how many days' depending on the scale of an outbreak. 🇨🇳 What is the '1335 Measure'? The '1335' protocol is used for responding to outbreaks and clusters. According to China's definition, a cluster outbreak occurs when three or more confirmed domestic cases occur within a certain period in the same household, school, construction site, community, or village. The '1335' represents the time required for the response in numerical form. Within 1 day, establish a risk zone and begin mosquito eradication. Within 3 days, complete door-to-door surveys in the core zone. Within 3 days, complete comprehensive adult mosquito eradication in the core zone. Within 5 days, reduce the mosquito vector density in the core zone to a safe level. Furthermore, in the alert zones, we will carry out environmental improvements and remove water puddles that serve as mosquito breeding sources, with the goal of reducing the Breteau Index (an indicator of Aedes mosquito larval density) to less than 5 within 7 days. In other words, instead of waiting to confirm cases before considering a response, this is a mechanism that manages outbreak response on a timeline of "1 day, 3 days, 5 days" from the very beginning. For larger local outbreaks, the "1113" protocol is used. Furthermore, for "local outbreak epidemics" where 10 or more domestic confirmed cases are reported within a certain period in the same street, township, or town, the response time is further shortened. This is where "1113" is used. Within 1 hour, that is, establish risk zones as immediately as possible. Within 1 hour, start door-to-door surveys in the core zone. Within 1 day, carry out comprehensive adult mosquito control in the core and alert zones. Within 3 days, control the mosquito vector density in the core zone. During the epidemic period, mosquito vector density will be monitored daily, and risk assessments will be conducted daily. Furthermore, "one report per day" will be implemented, and measures will be adjusted according to the epidemic situation. We will also strengthen the fever clinic system and the stockpiling of test reagents, and implement "test every fever case" and "dual fever testing". "Test every fever case" is the concept of actively connecting fever patients to testing according to the epidemic situation. "Dual fever testing" means testing for dengue fever and chikungunya fever, which have similar symptoms, at the same time. In the 2026 version of the prevention and control plan, it is clearly stated that both diseases should be "monitored together, tested together, and prevented and controlled together." Using mosquito density, not just "case numbers," as an outcome What is particularly interesting about this mechanism is that the response goal is not just about "how many patients were found." In the core zone, mosquito density is measured daily to confirm whether the vector mosquitoes are actually decreasing due to the measures taken. In other words, detect cases, establish risk zones, conduct door-to-door surveys, exterminate mosquitoes, measure mosquito vector density, and evaluate whether it has dropped to the target value. This is the cycle. Surveillance and vector control are integrated. The background for the appearance of the terms "1335" and "1113" in the September China CDC risk assessment is this 2026 version of the prevention and control plan. It is not just a slogan, but a mechanism that standardizes time targets for outbreak response. Zika virus also carries a high import risk Regarding Zika virus infection, 22 imported cases have been reported from January to the end of August 2026. In August alone, there were 7 cases reported from Fujian, Chongqing, Shanghai, Hainan, and Henan, and the countries considered to be the sources of infection include Thailand, Malaysia, Vietnam, and Papua New Guinea. The China CDC assesses that the risk of importation remains high due to the high volume of human traffic between China and Southeast Asia and the Western Pacific region, as well as the approaching Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day travel seasons. Here too, the China CDC is calling for "co-prevention of multiple mosquito-borne diseases" rather than completely separate measures for each disease. This is an approach that uses vector mosquito control, early diagnosis in medical institutions, and health education for travelers as a common foundation for multiple mosquito-borne diseases. Mpox increased by 80% in August compared to the previous month Regarding mpox, the cumulative number of confirmed cases from June 2023 to the end of August 2026 is 3,852. In August 2026, 153 cases were reported, an 80% increase from July. The China CDC predicts that the epidemic will continue to be seen mainly among men who have sex with men and will fluctuate at a low level in the short term. On the other hand, it states that the risks of both overseas importation and domestic secondary transmission will continue. Of particular note is that the measures include sewage surveillance. The China CDC is calling for the strengthening of sewage monitoring at key facilities in pilot cities, in addition to sewage monitoring of incoming flights to key areas. It combines environmental surveillance with case reporting and epidemiological investigations. New subtype influenza such as H9N2 may continue to have "sporadic cases" In August 2026, 3 cases of human infection with H9N2 avian influenza were reported. news.content: Homepage Latest News Cuba News Miami News Blackouts today Informal Exchange Rate Videos Entertainment Sports International News Opinion CiberCuba Interviews United States Cuisine Florida Spain Culture Engine Readings Tourism History Nature Health Close the sidebar ESENFRIT Pharmacists could administer the vaccine against chikungunya in Florida Latest News By CiberCuba Editorial Team Friday, September 18, 2026 - 7:08 PM Mosquito Aedes aegyptiPhoto © Radio Guantánamo The Florida Department of Health (DOH) proposed to expand the list of vaccines that pharmacists can administer to include immunization against chikungunya, a viral disease transmitted by mosquitoes that has resulted in a high number of reports in the state this year. The proposal was announced this Friday by Telemundo 51, based on a report from News Service of Florida. The change would amend rule 64B16-27.650, which regulates the additional immunizations that pharmacists can administer in the state. The official notice published by the Florida Board of Pharmacy confirms that it is proposing to modify the rule to add new vaccines and establishes a public comment period that will remain open until October 8. According to the report on notifiable diseases from the DOH cited by News Service of Florida, Florida has recorded 189 cases of chikungunya so far in 2026. Of these, 120 are from Miami-Dade and around 92 were reported in January. Chikungunya is a viral infection primarily transmitted by the Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, both of which are present in Florida. It can cause fever and intense joint pain, and due to the similarity of its symptoms, it can be mistaken for dengue or Zika. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) currently state that the VIMKUNYA vaccine, made with virus-like particles and approved for individuals aged 12 and older, is available in the United States. The recommendation mainly focuses on specific travelers at risk of exposure and laboratory workers, which is why Florida's proposal would expand the locations where it could be administered, but it does not make the vaccine a routine immunization for the entire population. Epidemiological data from the DOH also indicates that not all chikungunya cases involve transmission within Florida. In its weekly arbovirus surveillance report for the period from September 6 to September 12, the agency recorded 66 cases linked to international travel and one locally acquired case, the latter in Miami-Dade with symptom onset in August. That weekly series uses a different epidemiological classification than the report on notifiable diseases cited by News Service of Florida, so the figures are not directly comparable. The proposal also arrives amidst a particularly active season for other mosquito-borne diseases in Florida. This Friday, the Health Department in Orange County confirmed two new locally acquired cases of dengue and announced that, along with mosquito control authorities, it has intensified treatments in the affected communities. The latest state report available as of September 12 accounted for 152 cases of dengue acquired within Florida, primarily in Hillsborough, as well as Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco, and Pinellas. It also recorded 186 cases associated with international travel. The situation had already raised alarms in the southern part of the state. In August, the Health Department confirmed a locally acquired case of dengue in Miami-Dade and activated joint mosquito surveillance and control measures. At the beginning of September, the rise in dengue cases led to increased fumigation and monitoring in several counties in Florida, including Hillsborough, Pinellas, Orange, and Miami-Dade. It can cause fever and intense joint pain, and due to the similarity of its symptoms, it can be mistaken for dengue or Zika. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) currently state that the VIMKUNYA vaccine, made with virus-like particles and approved for individuals aged 12 and older, is available in the United States. The recommendation mainly focuses on specific travelers at risk of exposure and laboratory workers, which is why Florida's proposal would expand the locations where it could be administered, but it does not make the vaccine a routine immunization for the entire population. Epidemiological data from the DOH also indicates that not all chikungunya cases involve transmission within Florida. In its weekly arbovirus surveillance report for the period from September 6 to September 12, the agency recorded 66 cases linked to international travel and one locally acquired case, the latter in Miami-Dade with symptom onset in August. That weekly series uses a different epidemiological classification than the report on notifiable diseases cited by News Service of Florida, so the figures are not directly comparable. The proposal also arrives amidst a particularly active season for other mosquito-borne diseases in Florida. This Friday, the Health Department in Orange County confirmed two new locally acquired cases of dengue and announced that, along with mosquito control authorities, it has intensified treatments in the affected communities. The latest state report available as of September 12 accounted for 152 cases of dengue acquired within Florida, primarily in Hillsborough, as well as Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco, and Pinellas. It also recorded 186 cases associated with international travel. The situation had already raised alarms in the southern part of the state. In August, the Health Department confirmed a locally acquired case of dengue in Miami-Dade and activated joint mosquito surveillance and control measures. At the beginning of September, the rise in dengue cases led to increased fumigation and monitoring in several counties in Florida, including Hillsborough, Pinellas, Orange, and Miami-Dade. September 22, 2026 Saudi Arabia NewsThe PlaceThe SpaceWho's WhoKSA TodayGreen & Blue Middle East World Business InsightEnergyFinanceGiga-ProjectsMiningStartupsTourism & TransportEye On AI Media Lifestyle Art & CultureFashionOffbeatTravelEntertainmentFood & HealthThe Six Opinion Sport Saudi FootballSaudi Pro LeagueFootballMotorsportTennisCricketGolf Research & Studies Research PapersYouGovDeep DivePreachers of Hate Podcast LATEST NEWS/Middle East Pakistan interior minister in Tehran to discuss regional developments - officials You are here Home 309406 Study Warns Against Chikungunya Outbreak Short Url https://www.arabnews.com/world/archive-309406 Updated 1 March 2008 00:00 Mohammed Ashraf, Arab News March 1, 2008 00:00 THIRUVANANTHAPURAM — A study on the socio-economic impact of last year’s chikungunya epidemic in Kerala has warned that one more outbreak would have devastating effect on the state’s low-income people. Poor people have been the largest number of victims of the disease and the phenomenon is highly regressive on the well-being of the society at large and the low-income families in particular, it says. The study conducted by the University of Kerala, Virology Institute, Pune, N.S. Memorial Hospital, Kollam, and the city-based Population Health and Research Institute and Knowledge Synergy Systems suggests immediate implementation of a social health insurance scheme to ensure that families affected by such maladies do not find themselves financially devastated. “In more than half the chikungunya cases, the expenditure on treatment exceeded their meager monthly income. And around one-thirds of the infected-people’s work efficiency has been decreased and this has badly affected their capacity to earn a living as muscle/joint pains caused by the infection last for over a year,” it says. The study says the disease has had a negative effect on the life span of the affected person. “It’s shameful that the state lacked a good center for virology tests. In most of the cases, the virus in the blood sample ceases to exist when it reaches Pune for test. Hence, the results sometimes rule out the disease being chikungunya. The only virology center in the country is in Pune. Early diagnosis and immediate eradication of the virus is absolutely essential and this calls for the establishment of virology centers in different parts of the country, especially in a state like Kerala,” researchers K.T. Shenoy, V. Nandamohan and Leena K.V. said. As the number of chikungunya cases was significantly high during monsoon, it can cause a chaotic situation if not handled on priority, they said. Recently, researchers at Rajiv Gandhi Center for Biotechnology here have developed a new diagnostic test to distinguish chikungunya from dengue viruses. The test kit works as early as the second or third day of symptoms enabling early detection of the disease spread by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes that have initial symptoms of fever and joint pains. The test uses polymerase chain reaction (PCR) methods that rapidly produce thousands of copies of a gene. It contains two sets of gene probes - one common to all four types of dengue, and another specific to chikungunya. Chikungunya virus reappeared in India in 2006 after a gap of 32 years, with the Health Ministry reporting 1.3 million cases from 13 states. Officials estimate this year’s outbreak in Kerala affected 7,000 people. This time, outbreaks were of a different strain from the one reported in the 1970s as it carried a genetic mutation that helps the virus adapt better to the host mosquitoes and multiply more efficiently, which could be a reason for the severe outbreak in Kerala. Donate Now Health News Florida Florida health department moves to allow pharmacists to give chikungunya vaccine WUSF | By Rick Mayer Published September 17, 2026 at 11:47 PM EDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Unsplash A proposed rule would allow people to receive the shot at pharmacies. The Board of Pharmacy is accepting public comments through Oct. 8. The Florida Department of Health is proposing a rule that would allow pharmacists to administer a vaccine against chikungunya, a mosquito-borne illness that can cause fever and severe joint pain. Chikungunya can be difficult to distinguish from dengue and Zika, which can cause similar symptoms, according to the World Health Organization. Chikungunya is spread by the same mosquito species: Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, both found in Florida. Florida has reported 189 chikungunya cases so far this year, according to the Department of Health’s reportable diseases frequency report. Miami-Dade County accounted for 120 of those cases, with about 92 reported in January. The proposed rule would amend the state’s list of additional vaccines that pharmacists may administer. The vaccine would prompt the immune system to produce an immune response against chikungunya virus, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Few vaccines are available for mosquito-borne illnesses. The Board of Pharmacy is accepting public comments through Oct. 8. Click here for a form to leave comments. news.title: Doctors urged to test for chikungunya as Hong Kong detects first local 2026 case - South China Morning Post
news.rss_summary_html: Doctors urged to test for chikungunya as Hong Kong detects first local 2026 case  South China Morning Post
news.excerpt_original: Doctors urged to test for chikungunya as Hong Kong detects first local 2026 case South China Morning Post
news.priority_tier_reason: 可信机构来源或已成功抓获正文
news.content: Doctors in Hong Kong have been urged to arrange blood tests for patients with symptoms of chikungunya fever, regardless of their travel history, after the city recorded its first local case of the mosquito-borne disease this year. The Centre for Health Protection issued a reminder to doctors on Thursday after a 55-year-old woman with no recent travel history was reported as Hong Kong’s first locally acquired chikungunya fever case in 2026. “To facilitate early diagnosis and timely public health intervention, please consider arranging diagnostic testing for any patient presenting with symptoms suggestive of chikungunya fever, regardless of their travel history,” the centre wrote in a letter to doctors. Testing for the mosquito-borne disease is free of charge at the public health laboratory service under the centre. View in App READ FULL ARTICLE The latest infected woman, who lives on Li Tak Street in Tai Kok Tsui, started to develop symptoms such as fever, headaches and joint pain in her fingers and wrist last Monday, followed by a rash on her face and body. She sought medical care at Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Jordan on Wednesday and was admitted on the same day for treatment. She was in a stable condition. Li Tak Street in Tai Kok Tsui. Authorities have urged people who had visited Li Tak Street or the nearby parks and were exhibiting symptoms to seek medical advice. Photo: Google Maps The woman did not travel during the incubation period, but recalled receiving mosquito bites at her residence and in areas around Cherry Street Park and Lok Kwan Street Park. The centre is still conducting an epidemiological investigation into the case. It urged people who had visited Li Tak Street or the two parks and exhibited symptoms such as fever, rash or joint pain to seek medical advice or contact the centre. The woman is Hong Kong’s third confirmed chikungunya fever case this year. The first two were imported cases reported in January. Last year, 82 chikungunya cases were recorded in Hong Kong, including 11 local cases. Mosquito activity, as measured by the government’s Gravidtrap Index, started to pick up in some areas in Hong Kong this month. In Sheung Wan and Sai Ying Pun, the initial index for September was 32.1 per cent, falling within the level three readings that indicated the distribution of Aedes albopictus mosquito was “extensive”. Aedes albopictus is a type of mosquito that can spread diseases such as dengue fever, chikungunya and the Zika virus. Aberdeen and Ap Lei Chau recorded an index of 26.9 per cent, also reaching the third-highest level in the distribution of mosquitoes under the four-tier system

news.content: CubaHeadlines Pharmacists May Soon Administer Chikungunya Vaccine in Florida Friday, September 18, 2026 by Olivia Torres Image of Aedes aegypti mosquito - © Radio Guantánamo The Florida Department of Health (DOH) is considering expanding the list of vaccines that pharmacists are authorized to administer to include the chikungunya vaccine. This viral disease, which is spread by mosquitoes, has seen a significant rise in reported cases in the state this year. This proposal was announced by Telemundo 51, based on a report from the News Service of Florida. The change aims to amend rule 64B16-27.650, which currently governs the additional immunizations that pharmacists are permitted to provide in Florida. The Florida Board of Pharmacy has officially published a notice confirming the intention to revise this rule to incorporate new vaccines. A public comment period has been established and will remain open until October 8th. According to the DOH's report on notifiable diseases, as referenced by the News Service of Florida, there have been 189 reported cases of chikungunya in Florida so far in 2026. Of these, 120 cases were in Miami-Dade County, with around 92 cases reported in January alone. Chikungunya is primarily spread by the Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, both of which are found in Florida. The infection can cause severe joint pain and fever, often being mistaken for dengue or Zika due to similar symptoms. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) currently offer the VIMKUNYA vaccine in the United States. This vaccine, containing virus-like particles, is approved for individuals aged 12 and older. It is mainly recommended for certain travelers at risk of exposure and laboratory workers. Florida's proposal would increase the vaccine's availability but does not suggest making it a routine immunization for the general population. DOH epidemiological data further indicate that not all chikungunya cases are the result of local transmission within Florida. In their weekly arbovirus surveillance report covering the period from September 6 to September 12, the agency recorded 66 travel-related cases and one locally acquired case in Miami-Dade, with symptoms beginning in August. This proposal emerges during an especially active season for other mosquito-borne diseases in Florida. On the same Friday, the Orange County Health Department confirmed two new locally acquired dengue cases and announced increased mosquito control efforts in affected communities. The latest state report, as of September 12, documented 152 locally acquired dengue cases in Florida, predominantly in Hillsborough, in addition to Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco, and Pinellas counties. There were also 186 cases linked to international travel. This situation has already prompted alerts in the southern part of the state. In August, the Department of Health confirmed a locally acquired dengue case in Miami-Dade, initiating coordinated mosquito surveillance and control actions. In early September, the rising number of dengue cases led to enhanced fumigation and monitoring across several Florida counties, including Hillsborough, Pinellas, Orange, and Miami-Dade. Understanding Chikungunya and its Impact in Florida What is chikungunya and how is it transmitted? Chikungunya is a viral infection transmitted primarily by the bites of infected Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. It causes severe joint pain and fever, often resembling symptoms of dengue and Zika. What changes are being proposed regarding the chikungunya vaccine in Florida? The Florida Department of Health proposes allowing pharmacists to administer the chikungunya vaccine, expanding its availability beyond current recommendations which focus primarily on certain travelers and laboratory workers. How many chikungunya cases have been reported in Florida in 2026? As of now, there have been 189 chikungunya cases reported in Florida in 2026, with 120 of those occurring in Miami-Dade County. news.content: ___ Play Now Log InSign Up Florida News Listen Live National News Weird News Local Traffic Local Weather Get News Alerts Florida News Florida May Let Pharmacists Give Chikungunya Vaccines By Rob Garguilo Sep 21, 2026 Photo: MargJohnsonVA / iStock / Getty Images FLORIDA - Florida health officials are considering a rule change that would expand access to chikungunya vaccination through pharmacies. The Florida Department of Health has proposed adding the chikungunya vaccine to the list of immunizations qualified pharmacists may administer. The Florida Board of Pharmacy is accepting public comments on the proposal through Oct. 8. The change had not received final approval when it was announced. Chikungunya is a viral illness transmitted through bites from infected mosquitoes. Common symptoms include fever and severe joint pain, along with headaches, muscle pain, joint swelling and rashes. Symptoms can resemble dengue and Zika, making the illnesses difficult to distinguish without testing. The virus is spread by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. Both species are present in Florida and can also transmit mosquito-borne diseases. Florida recorded 189 chikungunya cases in 2026 before the proposal was released, according to state health data. Miami-Dade County reported 120 cases, accounting for most of Florida’s total. About 92 statewide cases were recorded in January. Federal health officials associate chikungunya cases in the United States with international travel. Vaccination is recommended for people traveling to areas experiencing outbreaks or elevated transmission. Eligibility can depend on age, medical history, destination and anticipated exposure. Most patients recover within one week, although joint pain can continue for months or years. Newborns, adults 65 and older, and people with health conditions face a greater risk of severe illness. There is no medication specifically approved to treat chikungunya. If Florida adopts the proposed rule, eligible patients could receive the vaccine from participating pharmacists before traveling to affected regions. news.source_body_en: Florida health officials are considering a rule change that would allow pharmacists to administer the chikungunya vaccine, aiming to expand access for travelers to affected regions. The proposal, which is still under review, has not received final approval. Chikungunya, a viral illness transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, has seen 189 cases in Florida in 2026, with Miami-Dade County accounting for most of these. Symptoms include fever, severe joint pain, and rashes, which can resemble those of dengue and Zika. While there is no specific medication to treat the virus, most patients recover within a week. The vaccine is recommended for individuals traveling to areas with outbreaks, and eligibility depends on factors like age, medical history, and exposure risk. The Florida Board of Pharmacy is accepting public comments on the proposal through October.

The Florida Department of Health is proposing a rule to allow pharmacists to administer a vaccine for chikungunya disease. Chikungunya disease, a viral infection, is a mosquito-borne illness that can cause fever and severe joint pain. It can be confused with dengue and Zika, which makes the illness hard to diagnose, according to the World Health Organization. analysis.brief_en: The Florida Department of Health is proposing a rule that would allow pharmacists to administer the chikungunya vaccine, aiming to improve accessibility. According to the DOH's reportable diseases frequency report, there have been 189 reported cases of chikungunya disease in Florida this year, with the majority, 120 cases, concentrated in Miami-Dade County. The proposal comes as part of efforts to expand vaccination services, particularly in areas with high incidence rates. While the exact number of cases and their distribution are reported, the proposal itself is still under review and has not been implemented. The decision to allow pharmacists to administer the vaccine is based on the need to address the growing public health concern associated with chikungunya, which is a mosquito-borne illness that can cause fever and severe joint pain. The disease is often confused with dengue and Zika, making diagnosis challenging. This initiative reflects a proactive approach to managing the spread of chikungunya and ensuring timely immunization for at-risk populations.

supplementary_news.content: ___ Play Now Log InSign Up Florida News Listen Live National News Weird News Local Traffic Local Weather Get News Alerts Florida News Florida May Let Pharmacists Give Chikungunya Vaccines By Rob Garguilo Sep 21, 2026 Photo: MargJohnsonVA / iStock / Getty Images FLORIDA - Florida health officials are considering a rule change that would expand access to chikungunya vaccination through pharmacies. The Florida Department of Health has proposed adding the chikungunya vaccine to the list of immunizations qualified pharmacists may administer. The Florida Board of Pharmacy is accepting public comments on the proposal through Oct. 8. The change had not received final approval when it was announced. Chikungunya is a viral illness transmitted through bites from infected mosquitoes. Common symptoms include fever and severe joint pain, along with headaches, muscle pain, joint swelling and rashes. Symptoms can resemble dengue and Zika, making the illnesses difficult to distinguish without testing. The virus is spread by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. Both species are present in Florida and can also transmit mosquito-borne diseases. Florida recorded 189 chikungunya cases in 2026 before the proposal was released, according to state health data. Miami-Dade County reported 120 cases, accounting for most of Florida’s total. About 92 statewide cases were recorded in January. Federal health officials associate chikungunya cases in the United States with international travel. Vaccination is recommended for people traveling to areas experiencing outbreaks or elevated transmission. Eligibility can depend on age, medical history, destination and anticipated exposure. Most patients recover within one week, although joint pain can continue for months or years. Newborns, adults 65 and older, and people with health conditions face a greater risk of severe illness. There is no medication specifically approved to treat chikungunya. If Florida adopts the proposed rule, eligible patients could receive the vaccine from participating pharmacists before traveling to affected regions. Donate Now Health News Florida Florida health department moves to allow pharmacists to give chikungunya vaccine WUSF | By Rick Mayer Published September 17, 2026 at 11:47 PM EDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Unsplash A proposed rule would allow people to receive the shot at pharmacies. The Board of Pharmacy is accepting public comments through Oct. 8. The Florida Department of Health is proposing a rule that would allow pharmacists to administer a vaccine against chikungunya, a mosquito-borne illness that can cause fever and severe joint pain. Chikungunya can be difficult to distinguish from dengue and Zika, which can cause similar symptoms, according to the World Health Organization. Chikungunya is spread by the same mosquito species: Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, both found in Florida. Florida has reported 189 chikungunya cases so far this year, according to the Department of Health’s reportable diseases frequency report. Miami-Dade County accounted for 120 of those cases, with about 92 reported in January. The proposed rule would amend the state’s list of additional vaccines that pharmacists may administer. The vaccine would prompt the immune system to produce an immune response against chikungunya virus, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Few vaccines are available for mosquito-borne illnesses. The Board of Pharmacy is accepting public comments through Oct. 8. Click here for a form to leave comments. supplementary_news.content_title: Dengue fever and other mosquito-borne illnesses surging in Florida
supplementary_news.content: Mosquito bites can be more than a nuisance this summer — they can make you sick. Florida has become a hotbed for mosquito-borne dieases, reporting hundreds of cases of dengue fever, chikungunya fever, and even West Nile virus. The state leads the nation in dengue cases this year with 270 reported. Increasingly, residents aren't just acquiring the virus while traveling abroad — they are getting bitten right at home. Mosquito control experts note that peak dengue season runs from July through September. As many as 111 people as of early September have contracted locally acquired dengue in six Florida counties this year. While eight of these cases were in Miami-Dade and Palm Beach counties, a striking 95 occurred in Hillsborough County, where mosquito control teams are working overtime and ramping up spraying. The death of an 80-year-old South Tampa woman may be linked to a dengue infection. A common dengue symptom is a sudden high fever starting four to 10 days after a bite, followed by a skin rash a few days later. Treatment is limited to rest, fluids, and pain relievers. "There is no cure or antiviral medications for dengue," said Dr. Rana Chakraborty, division chief in Pediatric Infectious Diseases at the University of Miami. Many infected individuals remain completely unaware. "A lot of people can get bitten, acquire dengue, and nothing happens to them," Chakraborty said. "Only a fraction have symptoms." For about 1 in 20 people, dengue progresses to a severe level — triggering repeated vomiting, nosebleeds, stomach pain, and organ failure — often requiring hospitalization. While many species of mosquito inhabit Florida, only two transmit dengue: Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. Recognizable by their dark bodies and distinct white-striped legs, these daytime biters peak just after sunrise and before sunset. They also transmit Zika, yellow fever, and chikungunya. County workers across the state are battling populations by setting traps in parks and neighborhoods, focusing heavily on areas with confirmed cases: • Palm Beach County (currently under a mosquito-borne illness advisory): Stepped up surveillance and prevention efforts. • Miami-Dade County (under a mosquito-borne illness alert): Added wastewater surveillance to track virus spread. • Broward County: Operates a robust surveillance, trapping, and targeted spraying program using patented technology. "We are working with the Department of Health and every time we have a suspected case of dengue, they contact us, and we spray heavily around the blocks that could be impacted," said Adriana Toro, Broward County's assistant director of mosquito control. Toro noted that while travel-related cases are unavoidable, Broward has successfully controlled local transmission using patented turbine technology to spray large areas and test mosquito-breeding drains. "We have been proactive on the preventive side instead of waiting for an outbreak," Toro said. Frequent global travel significantly drives case numbers. So far this year, 160 Floridians contracted dengue after traveling to endemic areas — most frequently Cuba. Mosquito experts point to hotter summers and increased rainfall as additional contributing factors. Beyond dengue, Florida has reported 60 travel-related cases of chikungunya fever, as well as two locally acquired human cases of West Nile virus in Alachua and Walton counties. "It is smart — especially around dawn and dusk — to have EPA-registered repellent on exposed areas of your body," Chakraborty said. Chakraborty added that Miami-Dade's wastewater sampling aids proactive monitoring, anticipating additional cases as post-summer travel resumes. Public health officials are urging residents to take immediate preventive action. "Use insect repellent, cover up when possible, and remove standing water around your home. Individual prevention helps protect you and your community," the Florida Department of Health has urged. Pet owners can breathe a slight sigh of relief regarding their animals. supplementary_news.content_title: Column: Mosquitoes are making Los Angeles summers a living hell
supplementary_news.content: Click here to listen to this article - Share via See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred Two weeks ago, after a hot and humid summer of mosquito-induced hell, I decided I would spend whatever amount it took to get rid of the rapacious little creatures. Which is how I found myself in the bug aisle of Home Depot, staring at a wide array of products under a banner that read “Mosquitoes.” By the time I had finished loading up my cart, I had about $300 worth of chemical repellents for my skin, citronella candles, mosquito coils, a lantern-size ultraviolet zapper, a tennis-racket size ultraviolet zapper, two rechargeable Thermacell anti-mosquito misters and one butane-powered Thermacell mosquito banisher. Overkill? I think not! As I type this in my (unairconditioned) dining room, next to an open sliding glass door, I am running an electric fan pointing directly at my ankles in order to discourage the mosquitoes known as “ankle-biters” from attacking my bare legs. It didn’t used to be like this. Twenty or so years ago, our local mosquitoes were pretty mellow. But new, invasive species have exploded across Southern California in the last decade, making life hell for those of us who want nothing more than to sit on our decks in the shade enjoying our enviable weather. No time of day is safe. The tiny ankle biters are diurnal, which means they are active during the day — usually at dawn and dusk, said Karthikeyan Chandrasegaran, a UC Irvine ecologist who studies the bloodthirsty little beasts. The mosquitoes that carry West Nile virus and malaria, by contrast, are nocturnal. And they are wily. “If you swat at a mosquito and miss it, they are likely to understand something about it,” Chandrasegaran told me. “The next time they are going to try to bite you, they’re probably going to attack you in a different region. And they modify their flight trajectory depending on where they expect the swat to come from.” The biological response to a bite is well understood: When a female mosquito sticks her proboscis into, say, my ankle in search of tasty blood to nourish her eggs, her saliva unleashes an anti-coagulant that makes it easier to drain me. My body perceives her saliva as a foreign object and releases a counter-measure in the form of histamines, which send a signal to my brain that I am under attack, which my brain then interprets as an intense almost full-body itch, and screams that only an insane amount of scratching will help. And so I scratch and scratch against my ever-thinning, soon-to-be-bloody skin. I slather the bites with hydrocortisone cream. I rub on lidocaine. And I continue to itch and scratch until I slap on an ice pack to freeze my discomfort away. I have literally walked around my house this summer with baggies full of ice cubes taped to my legs, ankles and arms. I look ridiculous. While I am worried about my comfort, I should probably be even more worried about contracting a deadly disease. Mosquitoes can carry malaria, yellow fever, dengue, Zika, chikungunya and, of greatest concern in these parts, West Nile virus. “This year has been really bad in Southern California,” Chandrasegaran said. So far, Los Angeles County public health officials have documented at least 100 cases of West Nile virus and five deaths linked to mosquitoes. Worry all you like about lions, tigers and bears — and maybe charging hippopotamuses — but the mosquito is in fact humankind’s apex predator, responsible for hundreds of millions of infections globally, and about a million human deaths a year. “The mosquito has killed more people than any other cause of death in human history,” writes historian Timothy Winegard in “The Mosquito,” his sprawling 2020 book. “The mosquito remains the destroyer of worlds, and the preeminent and globally distinguished killer of mankind.” Winegard implicates mosquitoes in the extinction of the dinosaurs, weakened by the pests before the meteor hit. Mosquitoes may have been a factor in the deaths of King Tut, Alexander the Great and Genghis Khan. Around the world and across the centuries, untold numbers of soldiers have fallen to mosquitoes, which have repeatedly altered the course of major military campaigns, including the siege of Yorktown during the American Revolutionary War and the Haitian Revolution, which overthrew French colonial rule and indirectly led to Napoleon selling the Louisiana Territory to the United States. (Haitians had some resistance to the yellow fever-carrying mosquito; French soldiers did not.) Rome’s mosquito-infested Pontine marshes — drained eventually by Benito Mussolini — played an outsized role in the history of the eternal city, forming a deadly natural barrier against invading hordes over the centuries. Mosquitoes, unsurprisingly, played a part in the transatlantic slave trade. Malaria was so prevalent in prehistoric Africa that people evolved sickle-shaped red blood cells as a genetic shield against malaria. Sadly, the ability to survive malaria made Africans more appealing and valuable to enslavers. In 2010, Janet Fang, a young intern at the science journal Nature decided to investigate what a world without mosquitoes would look like. The scientific consensus was that the abrupt extinction of mosquitoes would save so many human lives that it would outweigh whatever ecological damage their absence would create. Scientists speculated that mosquito-eating fish and birds would simply switch to other forms of protein. “Life would continue as before,” Fang wrote, “or even better.” Not everyone applauded the idea. “People were mad,” Fang told me Thursday from Silver Lake, where she and her toddler have been plagued all summer by mosquitoes. West Nile virus was recently discovered in one of the reservoirs near her home. “I never once super said, ‘Let’s kill all the mosquitoes.’ I thought it was clear that it was a thought experiment,” Fang told me. “But I was villainized.” Personally, I think she deserved a Pulitzer Prize. Bluesky: @rabcarian Threads: @rabcarian More to Read Insights L.A. Times Insights delivers AI-generated analysis on Voices content to offer all points of view. Insights does not appear on any news articles. Viewpoint Perspectives The following AI-generated content is powered by Perplexity. The Los Angeles Times editorial staff does not create or edit the content. Ideas expressed in the piece - The article portrays Los Angeles summers as increasingly unbearable due to explosions of aggressive, invasive mosquito species such as daytime-biting “ankle-biters” that now swarm yards and homes even in normally pleasant weather, a trend consistent with reports of unusually intense mosquito seasons driven by heat, humidity and rainfall across Southern California[1][2][8]. - It describes a personal descent into mosquito “hell,” marked by extensive purchases of chemical repellents, candles, coils and electronic zappers, to illustrate how residents feel compelled to spend significant sums and adopt extreme, sometimes makeshift measures simply to enjoy outdoor spaces[1][2]. - The article underscores that the problem is not just nuisance bites but serious public health risk, emphasizing that mosquitoes in the region transmit West Nile virus and potentially other diseases, and noting that county health authorities have recorded elevated case counts and deaths in recent seasons[4][6][9]. - Drawing on scientific commentary, the column characterizes mosquitoes as humankind’s “apex predator,” highlighting estimates that they are responsible for vast numbers of deaths annually and recounting claims that mosquito-borne disease has shaped global history, from ancient rulers to major military campaigns. - The piece suggests that new invasive Aedes species are central to the current crisis, describing how Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus have colonized urban California, breed in tiny containers of water, and are capable of transmitting viruses such as dengue, chikungunya, Zika and yellow fever[1][8][11]. - It reports expert explanations that recent extreme heat, humidity and standing water have created ideal breeding conditions, causing mosquito activity to start earlier and stay higher than historic norms, and conveying warnings that mosquito season now stretches across much of the year rather than a short summer window[1][2][9]. - The article invokes a widely discussed thought experiment about a world without mosquitoes, noting that many scientists interviewed in that work concluded that global mosquito extinction would likely save vast numbers of human lives with limited ecological disruption, a conclusion the column presents as morally compelling. - At the same time, it recounts backlash against such ideas, describing how the thought experiment’s author was criticized and “villainized,” and arguing that these reactions underestimate how profoundly mosquitoes degrade quality of life and threaten health in places like Los Angeles. Different views on the topic - Public health agencies and vector control districts in Los Angeles County acknowledge rising mosquito activity and West Nile virus detections but frame the situation as a manageable endemic risk, emphasizing that annual case counts, while above recent averages in some areas, remain in the dozens rather than the catastrophic levels implied by global mortality figures[4][6][7][9]. - These official communications stress practical mitigation over eradication, urging residents to focus on draining standing water, maintaining pools and using approved repellents, and suggesting that consistent community action can substantially reduce mosquito populations without resorting to extreme chemical use or calls for wiping out the insects entirely[1][5][7][11]. - Local news coverage similarly highlights that most West Nile infections are mild or asymptomatic and never reported, indicating that severe neurological disease and death occur in a minority of cases, and encouraging vigilance and prevention rather than panic about an omnipresent lethal threat[3][5][7][10]. - Reports from regional vector control experts point out that Southern California has always had a seasonal mosquito presence, typically peaking from late summer into early fall, and while recent heat and rainfall have intensified and extended the season, these sources portray the change as a serious but predictable consequence of weather and climate patterns that can be addressed through long-term planning[1][2][9]. - Guidance from state and county agencies on invasive Aedes species reflects concern but also caution, noting that while Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus can transmit several tropical viruses, large outbreaks of dengue, Zika or chikungunya have not materialized in California to date, and that aggressive surveillance, targeted control and public education are intended to prevent such emergence without advocating global mosquito extinction[8][11]. - Critics of the “kill all mosquitoes” thought experiment, as described in the article, object on ecological and ethical grounds, arguing that mosquitoes play roles in food webs and nutrient cycles and warning that deliberately eliminating an entire taxonomic group could have unforeseen environmental consequences that scientists do not yet fully understand. - Some public health voices also caution against viewing mosquitoes solely as villains, emphasizing that human land use, neglected infrastructure and climate change contribute significantly to current outbreaks, and that sustainable solutions require investment in environmental management, public services and climate resilience rather than relying primarily on household-level consumer products[1][2][5][9][11]

supplementary_news.content: Search En|El HOME PRESS RELEASES 104.9FM LOGIN Σύνδεση συνδρομητή Climate crisis and global warming affect different categories of infectious diseases, Prof Magiorkinis says GENERAL /Κυριακή 20 Σεπτεμβρίου 2026, 16:31:33 / Last Update: 09:07 / Source: ANA-MPA The climate crisis and global warming have already affected different categories of infectious diseases, Associate Professor of Hygiene and Epidemiology at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens (NKUA) Gikas Magiorkinis, said in an interview with the Athens-Macedonian News Agency’s radio station Praktoreio FM. "Particular importance should be attached to those transmitted by mosquitoes, as well as infectious diseases linked to the environment and interactions between humans and animals," Magiorkinis said. Focusing on Greece, he said that the main problem is mosquito-borne diseases. He also referred to corvids, such as crows, magpies and jackdaws, which act as important amplifiers of West Nile virus transmission and, as he notes, have even been found on major streets in central Athens. However he added that "West Nile virus, mainly from mid June to end of September, has now become a persistent summer public health problem, while dengue fever and chikungunya virus are showing endemic transmission in parts of Europe that, until a few years ago, were not considered typical transmission zones." 152 local cases in Florida By Josh Frigerio FOX 35 Orlando Orange County News Published September 18, 2026 12:51 PM EDT Share Copy Link Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Reddit Published September 18, 2026 12:51 PM EDT Orange County confirms 2 new locally acquired dengue cases 0:00 0:00 Orange County confirms 2 new locally acquired dengue cases Orange County health officials have confirmed two new locally acquired cases of dengue fever in Apopka, bringing the county's total to three cases and prompting a mosquito-borne illness alert. The Brief There have been 3 locally-acquired cases of dengue fever in Orange County, according to the Florida Department of Health. The two most recent cases were acquired in the Apopka area There have been more than 150 local cases of dengue reported in Florida, and 186 cases of international travel-related cases. ORANGE COUNTY, Fla. - There have been two more locally-acquired cases of dengue fever reported in Orange County, bringing the county total for the year to three, according to the Florida Department of Health and the Orange County Mosquito Control. County officials have now issued a mosquito alert and plan to target more areas with mosquito spray to reduce mosquito populations. New dengue cases reported in Orange County What we know: Officials said the two most recent cases were acquired in the Apopka area. What we don't know: Officials did not release specifics on the individuals who acquired the illness. More targeting mosquito spraying in Orange County What they're saying: "We are conducting targeted control measures and enhanced surveillance in Pine Hills, Apopka, and throughout Orange County," said Steve Harrison, manager of Orange County Mosquito Control. "While CDC guidance calls for targeted treatment of areas of concern, we are taking additional measures. Given the increased Dengue Fever cases we are seeing in other parts of Florida, we want to be proactive to reduce the risk of further local transmission in Orange County." By the numbers: According to the Florida Department of Health's latest arbovirus surveillance weekly report, which runs Sept. 6-12: 41 new cases of locally-acquired dengue in Florida; 152 cases reported year to date 26 new cases of international travel-related cases of dengue; 186 cases reported year to date What is dengue? Dig deeper: Dengue is a virus spread through bites from two species of mosquitoes, Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, according to Florida health officials. Both are found in Florida. When someone is infected, it can lead to dengue fever, a sometimes painful, debilitating disease. While rare, if symptoms are left untreated, it can be deadly. Dengue fever symptoms Symptoms typically appear 3-14 days after being bitten by an infected mosquito, and usually last 4-7 days. Symptoms are similar to those of influenza and other viruses: Sudden fever Severe headache Eye pain Muscle and joint pain Bleeding Vomiting and diarrhea Can it be deadly? Dengue hemorrhagic fever, a more severe form of dengue, is rare, but can be deadly if not recognized and/or treated with supportive care, according to the Florida Department of Health's website. Treatment There is no treatment for dengue fever or dengue hemorrhagic fever. However, people should manage symptoms and complications. Tips for avoiding mosquito bites What you can do: There are a number of mosquito-borne illnesses found in Florida, including West Nile, Eastern equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, as well as travel-related illnesses, like chikungunya fever, dengue fever, malaria, yellow fever, and Rift Valley fever. Health officials are urging residents to take steps to prevent mosquito bites: Use insect repellent on exposed skin or clothing Remove standing water to stop mosquitoes from breeding Keep doors, exterior windows closed The Source: This story uses information from news releases issued by both the Florida Department of Health in Orange County and Orange County Mosquito Control, as well as information on Dengue fever from DOH and the CDC. Please reference surfaced articles to validate AI summary Explore DeeperDive Full Summary Florida has reported over 150 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026, primarily in Hillsborough County, and health officials are urging residents to eliminate standing water and use personal protective measures to prevent further mosquito-borne infections. More than 150 cases of locally-acquired dengue have been reported this year in Florida, according to the Florida Department of Health, some in South Florida counties. Hillsborough County saw 134 of the 152 reported cases this year, while Miami-Dade saw seven, Orange County saw one, Palm Beach saw one, Pasco County saw two and Pinellas County saw 7. More than 150 cases of locally acquired dengue have been reported this year in Florida, according to the Florida Department of Health's Weekly Arbovirus Surveillance Report, some in South Florida counties. The report for the period from Sept. 6 through Sept. 12 says that "152 cases of locally acquired dengue and 16 mosquito pools have been reported from six counties" in 2026. From Sept. 6 to Sept. 12 alone, 41 cases of locally acquired dengue were reported in Florida. Hillsborough County saw 134 of the 152 reported cases this year, while Miami-Dade saw seven, Orange County saw one, Palm Beach saw one, Pasco County saw two and Pinellas County saw 7. Dengue can present as "a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches and joint pain," along with fever and "sometimes" a rash, according to the Florida Department of Health in Miami-Dade County. Symptoms of dengue will appear within 14 days of being bitten by an infected mosquito. Dengue is not contagious, and is transmitted via the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. How to best prevent mosquito-borne illnesses In June, Miami-Dade County encouraged residents to "take proactive steps" to prevent the spread of mosquito-borne illnesses, including "frequently checking for and eliminating any standing water." That's the best protection against "container-breeding mosquitoes," said a press release by the county, which are the "likeliest species to transmit the viruses that cause dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever," illnesses that are among those most commonly transmitted by mosquitoes. Standing water usually accumulates after rainfall or irrigation in items like potted planters, saucers, outdoor toys, coolers and boat/car tarps, according to the release. "As little as one teaspoon or bottle cap of water standing for more than one week is enough for mosquitoes to breed and multiply," according to a flyer provided by the FDOH. As for individual protection, mosquito repellent can help prevent bites while outdoors, especially between "dusk and dawn," when mosquitoes are most active. The county also suggests: Covering entrances to one's home, including windows and doors, with mesh screens. Wearing clothes with long sleeves and pant legs to "maximize skin protection." Regularly cleaning rain gutters to avoid water pooling within them. Filling up indentations in one's lawn, air conditioner drain areas and tree holes. Regularly replacing water in outdoor pet dishes and birdbaths. Requesting a mosquito inspection via the county’s online portal. As many as 89 cases of dengue have been reported so far this year, as against 80 in the whole of last year. The civic body, in coordination with public health officials, are executing widespread vector control interventions to curb proliferation of larvae and prevent outbreaks of dengue, malaria, and chikungunya. Tired of too many ads?go ad free now The corporation has expanded its workforce and deployed additional dedicated domestic breeding checkers (DBC) tasked with daily door-to-door inspections. They check residential premises for potential breeding grounds, while educating households on eliminating stagnant water. Sanitation teams have undertaken targeted initiatives, including clearing clogged drains. The city’s rain deficit has allayed fears of fever spreads, but activists warned against complacency. D Balaji, a professor in Madurai, said awareness needs to be spread in rural areas to cut down mosquito breeding. “The rise in cases during rainy months indicates that standing water in puddles and within private properties needs to be removed, rather than undertaking only fogging,” he said, pointing to areas like Thiruparankundram, Alanganallur and Usilampatti. District administration officials say there is no major cause of panic. “There is an expected rise in reports of viral fever and dengue this month,” said a senior health department official, adding there is no concentrated outbreak of viral fever or dengue, as cases are spread across the city. “Whenever a fever case is reported, joint teams comprising medical officers and sanitation personnel are immediately dispatched to verify the situation, collect blood samples, and set up local medical camps. A structured fogging schedule is executed at intervals following a confirmed report, incorporating both fixed-location and spot-fogging techniques to destroy adult mosquito populations,” said Dr Abhishek, assistant city health officer. “The fogging is done on the day of the reported case, the day after and one week after as well,” he added. “Puddles formed in potholes are also being quickly cleared as part of the response to the rise in illness rates,” a senior corporation official said. He added that officials are closely monitoring social media as well as official grievance redressal channels to rectify infrastructure-related issues. Tired of too many ads?go ad free now Government Rajaji Hospital has established special vector-borne fever wards fitted with protective mosquito netting. “We receive around one case of dengue and around 10 to 15 cases of viral fever every day,” said dean Arul Sundaresh Kumar. He added that cases come from other southern districts as well. Health inspectors stationed at PHCs continue to closely monitor fever trends across wards, ensuring that despite a marginal rise in viral infections, transmission remains scattered without localized disease clusters. supplementary_news.content: English News Local Mp Gwalior Gwalior Dengue Alert: Health Department Sets Up Isolation Wards | 2026 94 dengue cases reported in Gwalior: Health department sets up isolation wards at Morar and 1000-Bed Hospital Gwalior 5 days ago Copy link A health worker collects a blood sample from an elderly man. The risk of dengue and seasonal illnesses is steadily increasing in Gwalior district as water accumulates after the rains and the weather changes. According to recent data, the number of dengue-positive patients in the district has reached 94 since January. In addition, cases of chikungunya and seasonal fever have raised concerns among health officials. In view of the steadily rising number of patients, the Health Department has set up isolation wards at Morar and the 1000-bed hospital. Five isolation wards have been set up at the 1000-bed hospital. Two isolation wards have also been established at Morar District Hospital, where all arrangements have been made to accommodate patients. As for swine flu patients, seven people have tested positive for swine flu so far. Of these, two have fully recovered and returned home. The other five patients are still being treated in the hospital's isolation ward. A team of doctors is keeping a close watch on them. Patients and their attendants standing at the hospital counter to undergo tests Health department makes major arrangements Door-to-door larval survey: More than 20 special teams from the Malaria and Health departments are going door to door in urban and rural areas, checking stagnant water in coolers, water tanks and flower pots. More than 20 special teams from the Malaria and Health departments are going door to door in urban and rural areas, checking stagnant water in coolers, water tanks and flower pots. Larval destruction and anti-larval spraying: Wherever Aedes mosquito larvae are found, they are being destroyed on the spot and anti-larval chemicals are being sprayed. Wherever Aedes mosquito larvae are found, they are being destroyed on the spot and anti-larval chemicals are being sprayed. Special isolation wards in hospitals: Safe isolation beds have been reserved for dengue patients at primary health centres, including Jaya Arogya Hospital (JAH) and the District Hospital (Morar). Safe isolation beds have been reserved for dengue patients at primary health centres, including Jaya Arogya Hospital (JAH) and the District Hospital (Morar). Free testing and adequate platelet supplies: ELISA tests are being conducted free of charge for suspected patients. Instructions have been issued to maintain adequate stocks of platelets and essential medicines in blood banks. ELISA tests are being conducted free of charge for suspected patients. Instructions have been issued to maintain adequate stocks of platelets and essential medicines in blood banks. Fogging and public awareness: Fogging is being carried out in the affected areas with the support of the municipal corporation. People are also being made aware of the need to prevent water from accumulating around their homes. File photo of the isolation ward set up in the 1000-bed facility Health experts' appeal The district malaria officer and health experts have appealed to citizens to observe a 'dry day' every week. They should clean coolers, water tanks and old utensils. If symptoms such as high fever, headache or joint pain appear, they should not take medication without a doctor's advice and should immediately get examined at the nearest health centre
